cover.headline: I build things when the obvious solution isn't good enough.
cover.standfirst: I'm a software engineer and founder based in Nairobi. I work across web, mobile, AI and backend systems — usually somewhere between “this should be possible” and “okay, let's figure it out.”
cover.caption: Fig. 1 — usually somewhere between Nairobi, a laptop and a ridiculous number of browser tabs

who.heading: So, what do I actually do?
who.lead: I write software, design systems and occasionally convince computers to cooperate.
who.intro: Most of my work starts with a problem that isn't particularly technical.
examples: Someone has a process that's taking too long.
A business has information scattered everywhere.
A team needs a tool that doesn't exist yet.
who.close: I like figuring out what's actually going wrong, then building the simplest system that makes it better.

building.label: Currently building
building.note: Turning messy business processes into software people can actually use.

what.heading: I don't just build the screen.
body: A good product is rarely just a frontend.
There's the interface someone sees, the backend quietly doing the work, the database holding everything together — and all the weird little decisions in between.
I like working across those layers, because that's usually where the interesting problems are.

context.heading: A little context.
body: I didn't get into software because I had a five-year plan to become a full-stack engineer.
I got interested in building things, then kept finding problems that needed better tools.
That turned into software engineering, then startups, then AI — and now a slightly unhealthy curiosity about how systems work.
I'm still figuring things out as I go.
context.aside: Currently building, learning and breaking things — in roughly that order.

solves.heading: I like building for the real world.
solves.standfirst: Because real users don't behave the way the documentation says they will.

items.label: Event tickets
items.scenario: Thousands of people trying to buy at once. One inventory. No accidental overselling.

items.label: Mobile money
items.scenario: Someone paid, but the M-Pesa callback never arrived. They still get their ticket.

items.label: School systems
items.scenario: The internet isn't always reliable. The software still has to work.

items.label: Many schools, one system
items.scenario: Everyone shares the platform. No school ever sees another school's data.

items.label: AI at work
items.scenario: The AI does the busywork. A person still makes the call.

items.label: Studying
items.scenario: Answers come from your own lecture notes — and get checked against them.

figuring.heading: Things I'm figuring out.
figuring.intro: Not a list of answers. Just the questions I keep coming back to.
questions: How do you make AI useful without making people learn AI?
How do you build software that survives unreliable internet?
How do you keep a multi-tenant system genuinely isolated?
When should a business automate something, and when should it just fix the process?

for.heading: People I like building with.

people.text: People running businesses with messy processes
Founders with an idea they can't quite explain yet
People who know what they need, but not how to build it

people.quote: There has to be a better way to do this.

for.tail: If you're nodding along, we should probably talk.
